narrative:
Your application was denied because the prediction estimated a 63% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That does not mean failure is certain; it means the assessment placed you above the school’s risk threshold for admission.

The strongest factor was your third-year class-rank decile. At decile 2, you were well below the average of about 5.8 among accepted students, and this pushed the prediction most strongly toward bar-exam failure. The second most influential factor was your LSAT score. At 35, it was somewhat below the accepted-student average of about 37.2, but in this case it worked in your favor and pushed toward passing. The third factor was your first-year class-rank decile. At decile 3, compared with an accepted-student average of 6, it also pushed toward failure, though less strongly than your third-year rank.

To move forward, ask for a human review of the decision and submit a concise explanation of any circumstances affecting your early class ranks. Ask whether a stronger LSAT retake, additional coursework, or a bar-readiness plan could be considered. If the denial is final, seek admissions counseling and prioritize programs that review applicants holistically rather than relying mainly on a predicted bar outcome.
